Consult Summary:
- One-line: Active, athletic patient with 2-week history of right knee pain and mechanical symptoms (clicking, activity-related pain) after increased running; clinical impression favors meniscal pathology or patellofemoral pain syndrome, with plan for physio evaluation and conservative management.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Right knee pain with clicking for ~2 weeks, worsened by longer runs; difficulty running longer distances for marathon training.
- Symptom timeline and pattern: Pain begins after about 20 minutes of running (approximately mile 2–3); intermittent giving-way sensations but no true instability; clicking with knee movement; transient swelling after the first run that resolved with ice; current knee not swollen at rest.
- Associated symptoms: Occasional tingling in right toes after running; no persistent redness, warmth, fever; no difficulty walking normally; no locking reported.
- Past medical history: Prior ice-hockey injury with a bruise several months ago; prior isolated UTI with ED evaluation; generally healthy; farsighted with prior LASIK.
- Medications and allergies: Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN (joint discomfort); Aleve (NSAID); Melatonin; Vitamin D; Xanax PRN; cannabis; no known drug allergies documented.
- Social/preventive health: Active marathon training; London resident; uses ice for injuries; no tobacco; no significant alcohol use described.
- Relevant negatives: No left knee symptoms; ROM reported as full (able to straighten and fully flex); no systemic symptoms.

Examination:
- Observed findings: Not all objective exam details documented. Patient reports transient swelling after initial run; currently no knee swelling. ROM described as full (can fully straighten and fully flex). No current locking or instability reported. Pain localized to knee with activity; crepitus/clicking described by patient.
- Vital signs: not provided.
- Additional notes: No definitive focal joint-line tenderness documented in transcript; physical exam to be completed by physiotherapist or in-clinic evaluation.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression: Likely overuse-related intra-articular knee pathology—most plausibly meniscal tear (traumatic or degenerative) given mechanical symptoms (clicking, pain with flexion/extension, activity-related onset) and prior knee injury; patellofemoral pain syndrome also plausible given pain with knee bending and running; osteoarthritis remains possible but less likely at this age without morning stiffness or persistent swelling.
- Supporting rationale from transcript and DDx: 
  - Evidence for meniscal pathology: clicking with movement, pain after several minutes of running, prior knee trauma, transient swelling after initial run.
  - Evidence for PFPS: pain with loading on the knee during running and activities such as abdominal movements, possible crepitus.
- Rank order (top 2–3): 
  1) Meniscal tear (traumatic or degenerative) — reasoning aligned with mechanism and mechanical symptoms.
  2) Patellofemoral pain syndrome / chondromalacia patellae — rationale: activity-related knee pain with loading and crepitus.
  3) Osteoarthritis of the knee — possible given age and activity, but less likely without inflammatory symptoms or morning stiffness.

Note on differential vs transcript: Some items in the provided broader Ddx (vascular/compartment syndrome, ITBS, ACL/LCL injuries, etc.) are not supported by the current transcript findings; these are acknowledged as less likely in this context. Conflict noted with non-supportive items (see Plan/Quality Checks).

Plan:
- Symptom management and activity modification:
  - Continue ice therapy to the knee as tolerated; emphasize early and frequent icing for inflammation reduction.
  - Ease up on running; if pain persists or worsens with activity, avoid running until reassessment.
- Pharmacologic management:
  - Continue NSAIDs as needed but transition to a regular, stronger anti-inflammatory agent (prescribed for regular use) and avoid concurrent ibuprofen. Take with food.
  - Pharmacy-directed prescription has been sent for the stronger anti-inflammatory.
- Referrals and investigations:
  - Refer to physiotherapist for comprehensive knee evaluation and rehabilitation plan (long-form assessment and treatment). This is the preferred initial step per clinician guidance.
  - Imaging: plan to consider knee imaging if exam suggests intra-articular pathology or if persistent symptoms with mechanical signs (e.g., swelling, warmth, locking) develop; MRI may be considered if indicated after physio assessment.
- Safety net and follow-up:
  - If knee swells, becomes hot/red, fever develops, or the knee locks and cannot bend/straighten, seek urgent medical care.
  - If symptoms persist despite physiotherapy and conservative management, arrange clinic evaluation and discuss imaging options.
- Additional context from DDx (consistent with transcript): The plan aligns with addressing suspected meniscal injury or PFPS and avoids premature imaging until physical assessment confirms need.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements clinically expected for a knee consult:
  - Allergies: not documented.
  - Current medications list incomplete in the plan (documented meds present; confirmation of all OTCs and supplements suggested).
  - Vital signs: not provided.
  - Formal knee exam details (joint line tenderness, effusion grading, ligamentous stability) not completed in the transcript; to be obtained by physiotherapist or in-clinic exam.
  - Imaging results (none yet): none available; indications for MRI/X-ray not yet established beyond plan.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - DDx includes vascular/CECS/PAES/etc. not supported by transcript findings; conflict noted. The plan emphasizes musculoskeletal etiologies with appropriate non-emergent workup; urgent vascular causes are not indicated by current presentation.
- Transcript quality:
  - Content is largely coherent but lacks objective exam details and vitals; relies on patient-reported symptoms and clinician guidance. Sufficient to guide initial management and referral but incomplete for definitive diagnosis without physical examination or imaging.

Document quality:
- Allergies: none documented.
- Medications: several NSAIDs used; a stronger anti-inflammatory prescribed; confirm all current meds at next visit.
- Follow-up plan: defined (physiotherapy assessment; imaging if indicated; urgent care if red flags).
- Clarity of information: generally adequate for initial management; additional objective exam data needed.

End of note.
